binders: A real parameter p equipped with a proof that 0 ≤ p ≤ 1.
hypotheses: 4000 ln(n) ≤ (n−1)p, where n is viewed as a real number.
conclusions: Under the binomial random graph measure on simple graphs with vertex set Fin n and edge parameter p, the set of graphs G for which every vertex v satisfies `|deg_G(v) − (n−1)p| < (n−1)p/10` has real-valued measure at least 9/10.
mathematical_definitions: The vertex set Fin n consists of the n labeled vertices 0 through n−1.
The graph law is `SimpleGraph.binomialRandom (Fin n) p`, obtained from a Bernoulli measure on non-diagonal unordered vertex pairs via the edge-set map.
The degree `deg_G(v)` is the cardinality of the neighbor set of v in G.
The measure appearing in the inequality is `toReal(μ(E))` for the graph measure μ and event E.
translation.proposition_plain_english: For every natural number n at least 2 and every p in the real interval [0,1], if `(n−1)p` is at least `4000 ln(n)`, then a binomial random simple graph on the n labeled vertices has, with measure at least 9/10, the property that every vertex degree differs strictly by less than one tenth of `(n−1)p` from `(n−1)p`.

restrictions_and_vacuity_risks: The claim is conditional: it applies only when n ≥ 2 and the strong density condition `4000 ln(n) ≤ (n−1)p` holds; for other n and p the proposition asserts nothing.
Although p is nominally allowed to be either endpoint of [0,1], for n ≥ 2 the density hypothesis rules out p = 0 and may leave no admissible p for many smaller n.
The deviation inequality is strict, so graphs with a vertex whose deviation equals exactly `(n−1)p/10` are excluded from the event.
The conclusion literally bounds `Measure.real`, namely the `toReal` conversion of the event measure, rather than directly asserting an abstract probability notation.
All vertices must satisfy the degree bound simultaneously; this is not a statement only about a fixed vertex, an average degree, or an expected number of vertices.
No asymptotic quantifier, unspecified universal constant, or separate claim that `(n−1)p` is an integer is encoded.
ambiguities: The dossier stops at the one-level body of `SimpleGraph.binomialRandom`; the deeper construction and normalization properties of `ProbabilityTheory.setBernoulli` are not exposed, so the exact independent-edge probability semantics are not derivable beyond the displayed pullback definition.

The dossier does not independently state that the measured event has finite measure, although its use with the displayed binomial random graph law strongly indicates the intended probability-measure interpretation; `Measure.real` would otherwise have special `toReal` behavior at infinite mass.
